sections.title: How does the EORTC bladder cancer recurrence and progression calculator work?
sections.html:
The EORTC bladder cancer recurrence and progression calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports recurrence points in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (number of tumors, the tumor diameter and the prior recurrence rate).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as ta and T1. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as no and yes. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as G1, G2 and G3. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.

6 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the EORTC bladder cancer recurrence and progression calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Recurrence points=(cis r + grade r + number r + recurrate r + tumor diameter + stage r)
Probability of recurrence at 1 year=((cis r + grade r + number r + recurrate r + tumor diameter + stage r))
Probability of recurrence at 5 years=((cis r + grade r + number r + recurrate r + tumor diameter + stage r))
Progression points=(cis p + grade p + number p + recurrate p + tumor diameter + stage p)
Probability of progression at 1 year=((cis p + grade p + number p + recurrate p + tumor diameter + stage p))
Probability of progression at 5 years=((cis p + grade p + number p + recurrate p + tumor diameter + stage p))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The EORTC bladder cancer recurrence and progression calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the EORTC bladder cancer recurrence and progression calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns recurrence points. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the EORTC bladder cancer recurrence and progression calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter probability of recurrence at 1 year in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Probability of recurrence at 1 year opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (6 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Recurrence points = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the EORTC bladder cancer recurrence and progression calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
